# Hantavirus on a cruise ship, latest report: seven cases and three deaths. The MV Hondius will dock in the Canary Islands.

On the cruise ship dealing with a hantavirus outbreak, the MV Hondius, "from April 1, the date of departure, until May 4, seven cases (two confirmed and five suspected), including three deaths, were recorded." This is the latest report, also released via social media by the Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. [...] "Based on current information," the DG explained, "WHO assesses the risk to the global population as low and will continue to monitor and update the situation." The UN health agency, the WHO chief added, "is working with the countries involved and the ship's owner to provide support to passengers and crew. The coordinated international response includes thorough investigations, isolation and treatment of cases, medical evacuation, and laboratory testing." [...] Spain has allowed the cruise ship to dock in the Canary Islands, the WHO announced, while it remains stranded off the coast of Cape Verde in the Atlantic Ocean. "The current plan is for the ship to continue its journey to the Canary Islands." Spanish authorities "have indicated that they will welcome it in order to conduct a full investigation" and "of course, to assess the risks to passengers on board," Maria Van Kerkhove, acting director of the WHO's Department for Prevention and Preparedness for Epidemics and Pandemics, told reporters in Geneva. "The risk to the general population is low. This is not a virus that spreads like influenza or COVID-19. It's very different," she added.

# 7 Suspected Hantavirus Cases Aboard Cruise Ship MV Hondius

—

A serious public health incident is unfolding aboard the cruise vessel MV Hondius in the Atlantic Ocean, where seven suspected cases of hantavirus have been reported—including three deaths and one British passenger currently in intensive care, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Of these cases, two have been confirmed through laboratory testing; the remaining five are under investigation to determine whether they are linked.

## Ship Held Off Cape Verde Amid Quarantine [...] ## About Hantavirus

Hantavirus is typically transmitted to humans through contact with rodent droppings, saliva, or urine. It can cause severe respiratory illness—though human-to-human transmission is extremely rare. Among the three fatalities reported so far are a Dutch couple and a German passenger; it has not yet been confirmed whether all deaths were caused by hantavirus.

A 69-year-old British man is hospitalized in critical but stable condition at a hospital in South Africa, where infection with a hantavirus variant has been confirmed. Additionally, two crew members are exhibiting acute respiratory symptoms and require urgent medical attention—though the cause remains unconfirmed.

results.title: Hantavirus: Update on Outbreaks from the Four Corners to the MV Hondius - Private Practice Infectious Disease
results.content:
The most recent ANDV outbreak occurred aboard the expedition cruise ship MV Hondius. A published timeline of the first 10 cases documented symptom onset, laboratory confirmation, and outcome for each patient, with the earliest case occurring in early April 2026. The ship carried 147 people, comprising 88 passengers and 59 crew members from 23 countries . A total of 13 cases were identified, including eleven laboratory-confirmed and two probable infections, with three patient deaths. A 42-day quarantine period was subsequently completed, and more than 600 contacts were placed under monitoring, none of whom developed hantavirus infection after a 2-month follow-up period .

## 8.   Conclusions [...] A 2026 outbreak aboard the expedition cruise ship MV Hondius produced 13 cases and three deaths and appears to be winding down following quarantine and isolation.
 Nosocomial transmission of Andes virus to healthcare personnel has been documented only where personal protective equipment was absent or inadequate, underscoring the need for prompt transmission-based precautions.
 The mean incubation period for HPS is approximately 21 to 27 days (ranging from 9 to 40 days), and both Sin Nombre and Andes viruses carry high mortality. [...] led to 34 cases and 11 deaths. ANDV infection has an incubation period of up to 40 days; thus, exposed persons should be quarantined for up to 6 weeks. Health care workers are at risk for nosocomial infection and should use appropriate personal protective equipment, respiratory protection, eye covering, and double gloving, to reduce their risk for disease.
